Clinical Reference · Pulmonology

Spontaneous Pneumothorax

On this page
Air in the pleural space with no preceding trauma — the lung's own recoil collapses it. Primary (PSP) hits tall, thin, young smokers with normal lungs; secondary (SSP) arises on diseased lung (COPD, PCP, CF) and is far more dangerous. Tension is the can't-miss emergency: decompress before you image.
PSP: tall · thin · smoker · 15–34 y BTS 2023: symptoms & risk drive Rx, not size alone Tension → immediate needle/finger decompression First-line PSP: conservative or ambulatory High-flow O₂ speeds resorption up to 4×
Shared

Pathophysiology & classification

🧬

Mechanism — the story

In health the pleural space is a sealed, fluid-lubricated potential space between visceral and parietal pleura, held at a negative pressure (~ −5 cmH₂O at rest). That vacuum is the tug-of-war between two opposing springs: the lung's elastic recoil pulling inward and the chest wall's tendency to spring outward. The negative pressure is what keeps the lung glued to the chest wall and inflated.

A spontaneous pneumothorax is a breach in that seal with no external trauma. Air crosses into the pleural space either through a ruptured subpleural bleb/bulla (classic in tall, thin young men) or through areas of "pleural porosity" — microscopic disruptions of the visceral pleura in smoking-related respiratory bronchiolitis, where inflammatory cells thin and fenestrate the mesothelial layer. Once air enters, the pleural pressure rises toward atmospheric, the vacuum is lost, and the lung's own recoil collapses it inward — like a stretched balloon released. The larger the breach and the more air that accumulates, the more lung is lost.

Two things then determine how sick the patient gets. (1) Gas exchange: the collapsed lung is still perfused but not ventilated → intrapulmonary shunt and V/Q mismatch → hypoxemia (mild in PSP with a healthy contralateral lung, severe in SSP with no reserve). (2) The one-way valve: if the pleural defect lets air in during inspiration but seals on expiration, air accumulates under positive pressure → tension pneumothorax. Rising intrathoracic pressure shifts the mediastinum, kinks the vena cavae, and drops venous return → obstructive shock and arrest. Tension is a clinical, not radiographic, diagnosis.

The chest is a syringe with a spring-loaded plunger (chest wall) and a stretched rubber balloon inside (lung), sealed by suction (the negative pleural pressure). Poke a hole in the balloon or the barrel and the suction is lost: the balloon shrivels to its resting size. If the hole acts like a flutter valve — air sucked in but not let out — every breath pumps up the barrel until it crushes the heart's filling. That is tension, and the fix is to let the air out, not to take a picture first.
Mechanism cascade: loss of the pleural vacuum → collapse → hypoxemia, and the one-way-valve branch → tension → obstructive shock. Green nodes map each treatment to the step it interrupts.
The pleural cavity is a sealed potential space; losing its negative pressure unglues the lung from the chest wall.
Image: OpenStax — Body Cavities labeled.png, Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 3.0)
Apical subpleural blebs/bullae (here giant bullous disease on CT) — the rupture-prone lesions behind most PSP and emphysematous SSP.
Image: Hellerhoff — Vanishing lung Syndrom 68W - CR und CT - 001.jpg, Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)
Everything downstream targets one of three steps. High-flow O₂ attacks resorption: breathing ~100% O₂ washes nitrogen out of the blood, steepening the N₂ gradient from pleural space → capillary so trapped air is reabsorbed up to ~4× faster (baseline reabsorption is only ~1.25–2.2% of the hemithorax volume per day). Aspiration / chest drains mechanically evacuate the air. Pleurodesis and blebectomy attack recurrence by obliterating the space and removing the culprit lesion.
🗂️

Classification — the four buckets & the size question

TypeLung statusWho / causeWhy it matters
Primary spontaneous (PSP)Clinically normal lungTall, thin men 15–34 y; smoking (↑ risk ~9× women, ~22× men, dose-dependent); cannabis; FLCN/Birt-Hogg-Dubé; MarfanUsually well-tolerated; conservative/ambulatory pathways now first-line
Secondary spontaneous (SSP)Diseased lung, no reserveCOPD/emphysema (most common), PCP in HIV, CF, TB, LAM, lung cancer, Marfan/Ehlers-Danlos, catamenial (thoracic endometriosis)Small volume → big physiology; nearly all admitted & drained; higher recurrence (~40–56%)
Traumatic / iatrogenicVariableRib #, central line, thoracentesis, biopsy, barotrauma on vent (contrast only — not this guide's focus)Different pathway; occult PTX on vent can tension fast
Tension (any of the above)Progressive collapse + shiftOne-way valve physiologyImmediate decompression — clinical diagnosis

Size — measured, but no longer the primary trigger

BTS 2023 deliberately demoted size: symptoms and high-risk characteristics decide the intervention; size mainly informs whether an intervention is safe to attempt and helps track resolution. Still know the two conventions and the volume math:

Convention"Large" cut-offHow measuredVolume estimate
BTS≥ 2 cm interpleural distance at the level of the hilumHorizontal distance lung margin → chest wall at hilum on PA CXRA 2 cm rim ≈ ~50% loss of hemithorax volume (pleural volume ∝ radius³)
ACCP≥ 3 cm apex-to-cupolaVertical apical interpleural distance—
Light indexQuantitative %% = 100 − 100 × (lung diameter³ ÷ hemithorax diameter³)e.g. lung 9 cm, hemithorax 10 cm → ~27%
CollinsQuantitative %% = 4.2 + 4.7 × (A + B + C), where A = apical, B = mid, C = basal interpleural distances (cm)Validated against CT
Size ≠ symptoms. A 60% PSP in a comfortable, non-hypoxic 22-year-old can be observed; a 15% SSP in a hypoxic COPD patient gets a drain. The 2023 shift is the single most testable change from the old size-first algorithm.

Presentation & findings — and why

🩻

Symptoms & signs by frequency

Classic story: sudden, unilateral, pleuritic chest pain and dyspnea, often at rest, in a tall thin young smoker (PSP) or a known lung-disease patient who acutely decompensates (SSP). Frequencies below are approximate ranges from case series; color encodes how often you'll see each.

Symptom / sign~FrequencyWhy it happens
Ipsilateral pleuritic chest pain~85–90%Parietal pleura is somatically innervated; air separates the inflamed pleural surfaces and stretches them with respiration
Dyspnea / breathlessness~80%Lost ventilating volume + shunt; severity tracks underlying reserve (mild PSP, marked SSP)
Tachycardia (HR >100)~40–70%Sympathetic response to pain/hypoxia; >135 with hypotension is an ominous tension sign
Sudden onset at rest~60–70%Bleb rupture is not exertion-dependent — classically occurs sitting/sleeping, a useful history point
↓ Breath sounds ipsilaterally~50–70%Air layer insulates sound transmission from the collapsed lung to the chest wall
Dry cough~25–35%Pleural/bronchial irritation
Hyper-resonance to percussion~20–35%Air-filled pleura transmits a tympanic note; insensitive, specific
↓ Tactile fremitus~20–30%Air is a poor conductor of vibration from voice
Hypoxia / SpO₂ <92%~15–30% (higher in SSP)Shunt through the non-ventilated collapsed lung; a BTS high-risk characteristic
Tracheal deviation away, distended neck veins, hypotension<10% (tension)Positive pleural pressure shifts mediastinum & obstructs venous return — decompress now
Hamman's crunch (systolic crackle)<10%Air in the mediastinum (pneumomediastinum) crackling with the heartbeat
Subcutaneous emphysema (crepitus)<10%Air tracks into soft tissues — more with SSP, drains, or air under tension
Hypotension + distended neck veins + unilateral absent breath sounds + tracheal shift = tension pneumothorax. Do not wait for a CXR — needle/finger decompress immediately (see ICU).

Assess

When to suspect

🔍

Outpatient presentation & who is at risk

Most spontaneous pneumothoraces present to the ED, but a stable, minimally symptomatic PSP can walk into clinic or urgent care with a day or two of pleuritic pain that's now tolerable. Think of it in:

  • The PSP phenotype: tall, thin man/AFAB, 15–34 y, current smoker, sudden pleuritic pain ± mild dyspnea at rest, normal baseline lungs. Family history or bilateral/recurrent events → screen for Birt-Hogg-Dubé (FLCN).
  • The SSP phenotype: known COPD/emphysema, prior TB, CF, HIV (PCP), or interstitial disease who acutely worsens — dyspnea out of proportion to a modest-looking film.
  • Catamenial: recurrent right-sided pneumothorax in a menstruating woman within ~72 h of menses → thoracic endometriosis.
A young smoker with sudden pleuritic chest pain and a clear lung exam is a pneumothorax until a film says otherwise — auscultate both apices and percuss; unilateral hyper-resonance is the tell.

What to order & when

🧪

Imaging & labs — the order and what each changes

Erect PA CXRFirst test for every suspected case. Look for the visceral pleural line with absent lung markings peripheral to it. Expiratory films are NOT routinely needed (no added sensitivity). Sensitivity of erect PA ~83%.Initial
Point-of-care lung USFast bedside adjunct, esp. if supine/unstable. More sensitive than supine CXR (~88–90%). Absent lung sliding + absent B-lines; "barcode/stratosphere sign" on M-mode; a "lung point" is pathognomonic.Adjunct
CT chestGold standard. Reserve for: uncertain dx, complex/loculated air, suspected underlying disease/bullae, surgical planning, or distinguishing large bulla from PTX before drainage.Selective
SpO₂ ± ABGPulse ox on all. ABG if SpO₂ <92% or SSP — expect acute respiratory alkalosis with a widened A–a gradient; hypoxemia/hypercapnia flags poor reserve.If hypoxic
CBC, coagsOnly if an intervention is planned — check platelets >50 and correct INR toward <1.5 before a drain (see comorbidities).Pre-procedure

Treat

Management — BTS 2023 pathway

🧭

Symptoms & risk first — then choose

The BTS 2023 pleural disease guideline reorganized management around the patient, not the size. First rule out tension/high-risk features; then let symptom burden and patient preference pick the least-invasive effective option.

BTS 2023 spontaneous pneumothorax pathway (simplified). High-risk characteristics: haemodynamic compromise, significant hypoxia, bilateral, underlying lung disease, age ≥50 with significant smoking history, or haemopneumothorax.
1
Conservative (observation) — first-line for minimally symptomatic PSP, any size
If no high-risk characteristics and pain/breathlessness are mild.
▾
Air reabsorbs on its own at ~1.25–2.2%/day; if the patient tolerates it, letting the leak seal avoids procedure harm. The PSP trial (NEJM 2020) showed conservative care was non-inferior to intervention (8-wk re-expansion 94.4% vs 98.5%) with fewer serious adverse events and lower 12-month recurrence.
  • Selected outpatients with a small, minimally symptomatic PSP and good access can be observed at home with early review; larger or borderline cases are watched with a period of ED/observation-unit monitoring first.
  • Give analgesia and smoking-cessation counselling (below). Supplemental O₂ if admitted (speeds resorption).
  • Safety-net: return immediately for worsening breathlessness or chest pain. Repeat CXR at review (e.g. 2–4 weeks) to confirm resolution.
2
Ambulatory device — for symptomatic PSP, avoids admission
8F one-way valve device (e.g. Pleural Vent) in centres with expertise + follow-up.
▾
A small-bore catheter with an integrated one-way valve lets the patient go home while air evacuates. RAMPP (Lancet 2020): median hospital stay 0 days (IQR 0–3) vs 4 days with standard care — but more adverse events (55% vs 39%, mostly readmissions/device issues), so patient selection and follow-up matter.

Best for reliable patients with support and rapid access back to the pleural service. Review in clinic within days.

3
Needle aspiration — symptomatic, no high-risk features
14–16G cannula, 2nd ICS MCL or safe triangle; aspirate ≤2.5 L.
▾

Success ~50–70% in PSP; equivalent recurrence to a drain with shorter stay. If >2.5 L aspirated without resistance the leak is ongoing → place a drain. Re-image; if lung up and stable, many can be discharged with review.

4
Chest drain / admission — high-risk features or failed less-invasive care
Small-bore (≤14F) Seldinger drain; all SSP; see Wards.
▾

Any high-risk characteristic, all SSP, aspiration failure, or hemodynamic/oxygenation compromise → admit and drain. Details, technique and the safe triangle are in the Wards context.

Analgesia — treat the pleuritic pain so patients breathe

DrugStartTitrate → MaxWhy it worksIf contraindicated / alt
Acetaminophen (paracetamol)650–1000 mg PO q6hScheduled → max 3–4 g/day (≤2 g if liver disease/EtOH)Central analgesia; the safe backbone that spares opioidsFew; dose-cap in hepatic disease
Ibuprofen (NSAID)400–600 mg PO q6–8h with food→ max 2400 mg/day (Rx), OTC 1200 mgCOX inhibition ↓ pleural prostaglandins; excellent for pleuritic painNaproxen 500 mg BID. Avoid in CKD, GI bleed, CHF → use acetaminophen ± opioid
Oxycodone (opioid, breakthrough)5 mg PO q4–6h PRN→ 5–10 mg; lowest effective, short courseµ-agonist for pain the above can't cover; enables deep breaths & splinting reliefMorphine 2–4 mg IV; watch respiratory depression in SSP/COPD
The old worry that NSAIDs blunt pleurodesis is not supported by trial data (e.g. the pleurodesis RCTs) — NSAIDs are acceptable analgesia even around pleurodesis, and they reduce opioid need.

Smoking cessation — the single biggest recurrence-reducer

Smoking drives both the first event and recurrence; quitting can cut recurrence risk substantially. Offer pharmacotherapy at the index visit — every agent with a full ladder:

AgentStartTitration → Target/MaxWhy it worksCautions / alt
Varenicline0.5 mg PO daily × days 1–30.5 mg BID days 4–7 → 1 mg BID × 11–12 wk (may extend to 24 wk); set quit date ~day 8α4β2 nicotinic partial agonist — eases withdrawal while blunting the reward of smoking; most effective monotherapyNausea (take with food/water), vivid dreams; dose-reduce in eGFR <30
Nicotine patch (long-acting NRT)≥10 cig/day: 21 mg/24h; <10/day: 14 mgStep down 21 → 14 → 7 mg q4–6 wk over ~8–12 wkSteady nicotine replacement removes the withdrawal drive without inhaled toxins/tarCombine with short-acting gum/lozenge 2–4 mg for cravings — combination NRT beats patch alone
Nicotine gum/lozenge (short-acting)2 mg (≤24 cig/day) or 4 mg (heavier); or 1st cig >30 min after waking → 2 mg1 piece q1–2h PRN, ~9–12/day → taper; max 24 gum / 20 lozenge per dayRapid PRN top-up for breakthrough cravingsChew-park technique; avoid acidic drinks around use
Bupropion SR150 mg PO every morning × 3 days→ 150 mg BID (≥8 h apart) × 7–12 wk; quit date ~1–2 wk inDopamine/NE reuptake inhibition ↓ craving & withdrawal; option if NRT/varenicline unsuitableContraindicated in seizure disorder, eating disorders, abrupt EtOH/benzo withdrawal
Monitor

Follow-up, flying & diving

📈

What to recheck, and the activity rules

  • Repeat CXR at outpatient review (≈2–4 weeks) to confirm resolution; sooner if symptoms recur. Conservatively managed patients need a defined review with imaging.
  • Respiratory clinic referral for all — to confirm resolution, reinforce cessation, discuss recurrence risk, and consider CT/surgery in SSP or recurrent disease.
  • Air travel: defer commercial flights until full radiographic resolution; BTS advises a wait (commonly quoted ~7 days after confirmed resolution, longer post-trauma). Cabin depressurization expands residual pleural air.
  • SCUBA diving: permanent avoidance after spontaneous pneumothorax unless definitive bilateral surgical pleurodesis/pleurectomy with normal post-op CT and lung function — Boyle's-law expansion on ascent risks fatal tension/air embolism.
  • Counsel on recurrence risk: PSP ~30% (most within the first year), SSP ~40–56%; risk rises with each subsequent event.
Any trapped pleural air is a balloon that obeys Boyle's law — take it up in a plane (or down and up on a dive) and it changes volume. That's why "wait until it's gone" is a hard rule for flying and a lifetime rule for diving.
Interactions

How comorbidities change it

🔗

Comorbidity interaction table

ComorbidityHow it changes courseHow it changes management
COPD / emphysemaDefines SSP; small air volume → big physiology; higher recurrence & mortalityLower threshold to drain & admit; avoid high positive pressure; surgical referral earlier
HIV / PCPPCP causes necrotizing subpleural cysts → recurrent, bilateral, air-leak-prone PTXTreat PCP (TMP-SMX + steroids); expect prolonged leaks; early surgical/pleurodesis input
Cystic fibrosisPTX marks advanced disease & worse prognosisContact the transplant centre before pleurodesis (can complicate future transplant); manage air leak aggressively
Marfan / Ehlers-Danlos, Birt-Hogg-Dubé, LAMHigh recurrence; often bilateral; genetic implicationsConsider CT + genetics (FLCN); earlier definitive surgery; LAM → discuss sirolimus & early pleurodesis
PregnancyRecurrence risk rises; catamenial overlapFavor conservative/simple aspiration; involve obstetrics + thoracics; plan delivery (assisted 2nd stage); definitive surgery usually postpartum
Anticoagulation / thrombocytopeniaBleeding risk with any pleural procedure; haemopneumothorax is high-riskCorrect toward INR <1.5 and platelets >50 before elective drain; hold/reverse agents
Avoid / use with caution: positive-pressure ventilation, NIV/CPAP and high-flow nasal O₂ over an undrained pneumothorax (can convert to tension); nitrous oxide anesthesia (diffuses in and expands the space); high PEEP; aggressive early suction (re-expansion pulmonary edema); air travel/diving before resolution; and continued smoking.
Scores

Sizing & risk tools

🧮

What to compute vs. look up

Pneumothorax has no single validated severity score like CHA₂DS₂-VASc. Management keys off symptoms + high-risk characteristics (see the interactive selector below) and size estimation. The Light index and Collins formulas are the verifiable quantitative tools — both are built live in the calculator section. Interpretive size classification (BTS 2 cm, ACCP 3 cm) is also computed there.

  • MDCalc — general repository; no proprietary pneumothorax-severity nomogram to reproduce.
  • Use the Size & volume estimator and BTS pathway selector below rather than an invented point score.
Prevent

USPSTF A/B & recurrence prevention

🛡️

Whole-patient prevention for this population

Most spontaneous pneumothorax patients are smokers — the visit is a high-yield prevention touchpoint.

GradeRecommendationPopulation
ATobacco cessation: ask, advise, and offer behavioral + pharmacotherapy to all who use tobaccoAll adults who smoke (see cessation ladder)
BLung cancer screening: annual low-dose CTAdults 50–80 y, ≥20 pack-years, currently smoking or quit <15 y
AHypertension screening in adults ≥18 yGeneral adult population
BDepression / unhealthy alcohol screeningGeneral adult population — relevant in young smokers/cannabis users

Definitive recurrence prevention is procedural, not pharmacologic: VATS bullectomy + pleurodesis/pleurectomy drops recurrence to ~1–5%. Indications — see ICU/advanced. Vaccinate SSP patients per their lung disease (influenza, pneumococcal, COVID-19).

Escalate

When to send to the ED / admit

🚑

Red flags — don't manage in clinic

Any of: hemodynamic instability or tension signs (hypotension, distended neck veins, tracheal shift) → call 911/decompress; SpO₂ <92% or significant dyspnea; bilateral pneumothorax; known lung disease (SSP); age ≥50 with significant smoking history; haemopneumothorax; or failure of conservative care.
These map exactly onto the BTS high-risk characteristics — their presence means intervention/admission, not outpatient observation.

🛏️ Wards — admission, drainage & daily leak management
Admit

Who to admit

📋

Admission criteria & profile

Admit essentially all of the following:

  • All secondary spontaneous pneumothorax (SSP) — even small ones, because reserve is poor and deterioration is fast. BTS: admit all SSP for at least 24 h of observation and O₂ even if managed without a drain.
  • PSP needing a chest drain, or with failed needle aspiration.
  • Any high-risk characteristic (significant hypoxia, bilateral, haemodynamic compromise, haemopneumothorax, age ≥50 with significant smoking history).
  • Significant ongoing symptoms, social/geographic barriers to safe outpatient observation, or an ambulatory device requiring closer monitoring.
A "small" SSP is never reassuring — the number on the film understates the physiology. When in doubt with underlying lung disease, admit and watch.

🧪

Continuous SpO₂ + telemetryTrend oxygenation and HR; catch tension physiology early.Monitor

Treat

Acute management — evacuate the air

💊

Stepwise inpatient therapy

1
Needle aspiration — selected PSP without high-risk features
14–16G cannula; aspirate up to 2.5 L.
▾

Insert 2nd ICS mid-clavicular line or via the safe triangle; aspirate to resistance/cough or 2.5 L. Re-image. Success ~50–70%; if it fails or >2.5 L comes out, place a drain. Not first-line for SSP.

2
Small-bore chest drain (≤14F, Seldinger) — first-line drainage
All SSP, high-risk PSP, aspiration failure.
▾
A tube in the pleural space continuously vents air faster than it leaks, letting the visceral pleura appose the chest wall and the defect seal. BTS 2023 prefers small-bore (≤14F) — equally effective as large-bore for air with less pain (>14F hurts more).
  • Safe triangle: anterior border of latissimus dorsi (back), lateral border of pectoralis major (front), a horizontal line at the 5th ICS / nipple level (bottom), apex below the axilla. Insert just above the rib to avoid the neurovascular bundle.
  • Set to underwater seal, NOT suction initially. Confirm swing (respiratory oscillation) and bubbling (air leak). CXR to check position + re-expansion.
  • Add suction only if the lung fails to re-expand or the leak persists — high-volume, low-pressure at −10 to −20 cmH₂O. Early aggressive suction risks re-expansion pulmonary edema.
Small-bore chest drain at the bedside on an underwater seal — the first-line drainage setup (suction added only if needed).
Image: Johntex — Chest drain - bedside with fluids.jpg, Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 2.5)
CT (right) resolves an apical pneumothorax and its cause that a plain film (left) can under-call — used for uncertain dx and surgical planning.
Image: Cerevisae — Apical pneumothorax shown on CT and chest X-ray with left first rib fracture.png, Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)
Never clamp a bubbling drain — trapped air with an ongoing leak can build to tension. Clamping is only ever considered, briefly and supervised, to test for re-accumulation before removal.
3
Persistent air leak / non-re-expansion → surgery referral
Air leak >48 h (BTS 2023) or failure to re-expand.
▾

Refer to cardiothoracics for a persistent air leak beyond ~48 hours (historically 3–5 days) or a lung that won't re-expand. Also refer for: 2nd ipsilateral, 1st contralateral or bilateral spontaneous PTX, tension, haemopneumothorax, and high-risk professions (pilots, divers). VATS bullectomy + pleurodesis/pleurectomy is definitive (see ICU/advanced). Digital drainage (Thopaz) objectively quantifies the leak and can speed decisions.

Monitor

Daily management

📈

What to trend each day

  • Air leak: bubbling on cough/expiration (or the Thopaz number). Trend toward zero — decreasing leak means the defect is sealing.
  • Drain swing: respiratory oscillation confirms patency; loss of swing = blocked/kinked tube or fully re-expanded lung (correlate with CXR).
  • Daily CXR (and after any change): lung re-expansion, drain position, new effusion/RPE.
  • Oxygenation & work of breathing; pain scores (undertreated pain = shallow breaths).
  • Removal criteria: no air leak, lung fully re-expanded on CXR, drain not swinging from obstruction. Remove after a leak-free interval; many stop suction, observe 24 h, then re-image before pulling.
Escalate

When to call ICU

⬆️

Escalation triggers — numeric

Transfer/urgent ICU input for any of: tension physiology or haemodynamic compromise (SBP <90, HR >130); SpO₂ <90% despite high-flow O₂ or rising O₂ requirement; RR >30 with distress/exhaustion; rising CO₂ / respiratory acidosis; large haemopneumothorax with instability; a pneumothorax in a patient who needs (or is on) positive-pressure ventilation; or a massive persistent air leak with inadequate ventilation.
Dispo

Discharge & disposition

🏠

Readiness + where they go

Discharge readiness: lung re-expanded and stable on CXR after drain removal (or on a functioning ambulatory device with a clear follow-up plan); comfortable on oral analgesia; no supplemental O₂ requirement above baseline; smoking-cessation started; flying/diving counselling given; and respiratory clinic follow-up with a repeat CXR booked (≈2–4 weeks). Provide explicit safety-net advice to return for recurrent breathlessness/pain.

Home

The overwhelming majority — young, stable PSP; resolved or on a valve with follow-up.

Home health

Occasional frail/SSP patient needing O₂ management or wound/valve checks at home.

SNF

Deconditioned elderly SSP after a prolonged stay who can't yet manage independently.

Acute rehab (IRF)

Rarely — only if a complicated course leaves a reconditioning need with ≥3 h/day therapy tolerance.

LTAC

Complex ventilator-dependent/BPF patients needing prolonged (>25 day) specialized care.

Hospice / palliative

Pneumothorax as a terminal event in end-stage COPD/malignancy where goals are comfort (e.g., ambulatory Heimlich valve for symptom relief).
🫀 ICU — tension, the ventilated patient & definitive control
Admit

ICU triggers & the tension emergency

🚨

When it belongs in the unit

ICU for: tension pneumothorax or obstructive shock; refractory hypoxemia; a pneumothorax on (or needing) positive-pressure ventilation; massive persistent air leak/bronchopleural fistula with poor gas exchange; large haemopneumothorax; or peri-arrest.

Tension pneumothorax = decompress before imaging. Immediate needle/finger decompression. Per ATLS 10th ed (2018), the preferred adult site is the 5th intercostal space, anterior-to-mid axillary line (the old 2nd ICS mid-clavicular line fails in ~40–64% of adults because chest-wall thickness exceeds a 5 cm catheter). Use a long catheter ≥8 cm (≈3.25") — raising length from 5→8 cm lifts success ~70%→96%. In a peri-arrest or muscular/obese chest, go straight to finger thoracostomy. Every needle decompression must be followed by a definitive chest tube.
Large left pneumothorax with mediastinal/tracheal shift away from the affected side — the radiographic correlate of tension physiology (diagnose tension clinically, not on film).
Image: Photographed by User Clinical Cases 00:42, 7 November 2006 — Pneumothorax CXR.jpg, Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 2.5)
Monitor

Monitoring & access

🩸

Lines, labs, targets

  • Continuous SpO₂, telemetry, frequent BP (arterial line if shocked or on pressors / difficult to ventilate).
  • Serial ABG for oxygenation and CO₂ (BPF patients lose minute ventilation through the leak).
  • Chest-drain analytics: quantify air leak (Thopaz digital system) and watch the water seal; central access if pressors needed.
  • Serial CXR / bedside US: re-expansion, drain position, contralateral lung, RPE.
Support

Hemodynamic bridge in obstructive shock

💉

Decompression is the fix — this only buys minutes

Tension shock is obstructive — the definitive treatment is decompression, not vasopressors. Give a rapid IV fluid bolus to augment preload and use a pressor only as a seconds-to-minutes bridge while you get the needle/finger in.
AgentReceptors / mechanismDoseEffectWhen to pick
IV crystalloid bolusVolume → preload250–500 mL rapid, repeat↑ venous return across the obstructionFirst move alongside decompression
Norepinephrineα1 > β10.01–0.5 mcg/kg/min (titrate to MAP ≥65)↑ SVR, maintain coronary/cerebral perfusionBridge pressor of choice while decompressing
Epinephrineβ1/β2 + α10.01–0.5 mcg/kg/min (or code dosing if arrest)↑ CO + SVRPeri-arrest / refractory
The block is mechanical: positive pleural pressure collapses the great veins so the heart can't fill. Pressors can't overcome a kinked vena cava — they only preserve perfusion pressure for the moments it takes to release the air. Fix the mechanics.
Airway

The ventilated patient & air-leak strategy

🌬️

Minimize barotrauma; feed the fistula the least pressure

Positive pressure over a pneumothorax can convert it to tension and drives bronchopleural-fistula (BPF) flow. Any pneumothorax in a ventilated patient needs a chest tube. Then ventilate to minimize pressure/volume/flow across the leak:

Tidal volume
≤6 mL/kg IBW
lowest that maintains gas exchange
Plateau pressure
<30 cmH₂O
limit alveolar distension
PEEP
Lowest tolerated
high PEEP feeds the fistula
Driving pressure
Keep low
ΔP = Pplat − PEEP
Mode
Favor spontaneous
less positive pressure across leak
Permissive hypercapnia
Accept ↑CO₂
tolerate to protect the leak

Chest-tube suction: use the least negative pressure that keeps the lung up; excess suction increases fistula flow. For refractory BPF consider independent (differential) lung ventilation.

Suspected pneumothorax in a ventilated patient about to be transported? Decompress (finger thoracostomy) before the transfer — positive pressure + no monitoring in a lift/ambulance is how a simple PTX becomes an arrest.
Rescue

Definitive & rescue therapies

⚙️

Surgery, pleurodesis, valves, blood patch

Surgery — the definitive recurrence-preventer

VATS bullectomy/blebectomy + pleurodesis is standard for persistent air leak or recurrence prevention. Pleurodesis is by mechanical abrasion or apical parietal pleurectomy; pleurectomy has the lowest recurrence (e.g. 1/73 vs 8/34 for abrasion; overall post-VATS recurrence ~1–5%). Open thoracotomy has even lower recurrence but more morbidity — reserved for selected cases.

Chemical pleurodesis & air-leak adjuncts — agents & doses

Agent / therapyDoseAdd-onWhy / mechanismNotes / success
Talc (poudrage or slurry)2–5 g (PSP protocols often 2–4 g)Pre-treat with intrapleural lidocaineSterile inflammation fuses visceral↔parietal pleura, obliterating the spaceHistoric recurrence reduction 86–100%; poudrage at thoracoscopy vs bedside slurry
Doxycycline500 mg in 50–100 mL saline+ intrapleural lidocaine (painful)Tetracycline sclerosant → pleural symphysisShort-term success ~67%, long-term ~81%
Minocycline (post-first-PSP)Intrapleural adjunct after drainage—Chemical pleurodesis to cut first-recurrenceChen 2013: recurrence 29.2% vs 49.1% control
Autologous blood patch (BPF)50–100 mL autologous blood, or 1–2 mL/kg, instilled via drain—Blood clot seals the visceral pleural leak & promotes pleurodesisSuccess ~75–93%; option for persistent air leak
Endobronchial one-way valves (IBV/Spiration)Bronchoscopic placement to the culprit segment—Occlude airflow to the leaking segment while allowing distal air/secretions outPAL series ~82% success; earlier discharge — for poor surgical candidates
Intrapleural / infiltration lidocainePleurodesis: ~3 mg/kg (max ~250 mg) diluted; local infiltration max 4.5 mg/kg (≤300 mg) plain, 7 mg/kg with epi—Blunts the intense pain of sclerosant instillation & drain insertion250 mg > 200 mg for analgesia in trials

ECMO is a rare last resort for catastrophic air leak / refractory hypoxemia unmanageable by conventional means.

Re-expansion pulmonary edema after draining a chronically collapsed lung: incidence up to ~15.6%; risk with collapse >72 h, large volume, rapid evacuation >1.5 L, younger age. Prevent by avoiding early high suction and staggering drainage of large chronic collapses.
Downgrade

When to downgrade

⬇️

De-escalation to the floor

Downgrade when: hemodynamically stable off pressors; SpO₂ ≥92% on non-escalating O₂ (or baseline in COPD); no tension recurrence; extubated or off positive pressure; chest drain functioning with a stable or resolving air leak; and lactate/perfusion normalized. Not yet if: ongoing large air leak needing high suction, borderline gas exchange, or a lung not yet re-expanding.

ICU disposition: most step down to the ward for drain management and surgical follow-up; ventilator-dependent BPF patients may route to LTAC; align with goals of care in end-stage lung disease (a palliative ambulatory Heimlich valve can control symptoms at home).

Sources, trials & media

Landmark & practice-changing trials

Trial / studyYearDesign / NResultWhy it matters
PSP trial (Brown et al, NEJM)2020Open-label non-inferiority RCT; N=316; ages 14–50, first moderate–large PSP8-wk re-expansion 94.4% conservative vs 98.5% intervention (diff −4.1%, within 9% margin); fewer serious AEs & fewer procedures; recurrence ~8.8% vs 16.8% at 12 mo. Non-inferiority fragile if missing = failure (82.5% vs 93.5%)Conservative care is safe for many moderate–large PSP — size no longer forces intervention
RAMPP (Hallifax et al, Lancet)2020Open-label RCT; N=236; 8F Pleural Vent ambulatory device vs standardMedian hospital stay 0 vs 4 days (p<0.0001) but more adverse events (55% vs 39%), all 14 serious AEs in ambulatory armAmbulatory devices cut length of stay but require expertise & follow-up
Chen et al (Lancet)2013RCT; N=214; first PSP ± intrapleural minocyclineRecurrence 29.2% vs 49.1% at ≥12 moAdjunct chemical pleurodesis after a first PSP reduces recurrence
TIME1 (Rahman et al, JAMA)20152×2 factorial RCT; N=320; tube size & NSAID vs opiate for pleurodesisNSAIDs non-inferior to opiates (failure 23% vs 20%); smaller 12F tubes less effective than 24FDebunked "NSAIDs impair pleurodesis" — NSAIDs are safe for pleuritic pain
Ng et al (World J Surg)2018Comparative; N=107; VATS pleurectomy vs abrasionRecurrence 1/73 (pleurectomy) vs 8/34 (abrasion)Apical pleurectomy gives the lowest recurrence at surgery
Bense / Hallifax (epidemiology)1987 / 2018Case-control & population trendsSmoking RR ~9× women, ~22× men, dose-dependent; national incidence/recurrence benchmarksQuantifies the smoking driver and the recurrence problem
